items.title: Prayerful Looking
items.question: Weil wrote that one orientation of the soul sums up generosity, study, and faith; which three-word phrase names it?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. She treats sustained, loving regard as the substance shared by prayer, study, and care.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is attention is prayer. Generosity and study converge when the soul looks steadily rather than grasping.
items.lessonContent:
One faculty serves many practices.
Steady regard replaces grasping.
Quality of looking matters more than technique.
Practise sustained, loving notice.
Share this: give one task five minutes of undivided regard.

items.title: Open Hands
items.question: What two-word posture describes attention that waits without grasping at a result?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. The mind stays open and ready, refusing to seize meaning before it arrives.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is empty waiting. Forcing an answer too soon replaces attention with will.
items.lessonContent:
Waiting is an active discipline.
Emptiness lets reality enter.
Haste fills the space prematurely.
Hold the question open longer.
Share this: wait through one silence instead of filling it.

items.title: Wanting Nothing
items.question: A teacher watches a struggling pupil without steering toward the answer; what kind of looking does Weil hold up?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. The gaze wants nothing from the pupil, so the pupil's difficulty can appear truthfully.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is desireless regard. Wanting a particular outcome distorts what is actually there.
items.lessonContent:
Wanting bends perception.
Disinterest clarifies the object.
Watch without steering.
Let difficulty show itself.
Share this: observe one struggle today without trying to fix it.

items.title: Saying Yes Lightly
items.question: Facing an affliction she cannot remove, what consent preserves love without surrendering judgment?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. One says yes to reality while refusing to fuse with it.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is detached consent. Clinging and denial both refuse the world; consent neither flees nor grasps.
items.lessonContent:
Consent differs from surrender.
Detachment keeps judgment clear.
Say yes without fusing.
Meet reality as it is.
Share this: consent to one unchangeable fact without resentment.

items.title: Warm Observation
items.question: A friend in pain is met without advice or analysis; what simple orientation does Weil recommend?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. Bare, caring notice can hold suffering better than explanation.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is loving gaze. Advice often serves the adviser, while attention serves the sufferer.
items.lessonContent:
Presence can outweigh explanation.
Care shows in sustained notice.
Withhold the quick fix.
Stay with what is there.
Share this: meet one person's trouble with attention before advice.

items.title: Stepping Aside
items.question: What practice asks the ego to withdraw so that reality can appear?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. The self steps back so that the object is no longer crowded out.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is self-effacement. Ego fills the field of vision, so its withdrawal restores the view.
items.lessonContent:
The self can crowd out reality.
Withdrawal restores proportion.
Make room by stepping back.
Notice when you dominate the frame.
Share this: let one conversation be mostly about the other person.

items.title: Unmaking the Ego
items.question: Weil borrowed a startling term for undoing the creaturely self; what is it?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. The term names the voluntary undoing of the ego's claim to be central.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is decreation. It means yielding the imagined throne, not destroying the person.
items.lessonContent:
The ego claims the centre.
Yielding that claim frees attention.
Undoing is not destroying.
Practise small renunciations.
Share this: yield the centre in one small matter today.

items.title: Two Forces
items.question: Which pair contrasts the downward pull of necessity with the upward pull of the good?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. Everything sinks by one law and can be lifted by another.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is gravity and grace. Necessity drags downward while the good draws upward.
items.lessonContent:
Two pulls shape a life.
Name both to see clearly.
Necessity is not the whole story.
Notice moments of lift.
Share this: name one downward pull and one upward draw in your week.

items.title: Hard Embrace
items.question: What stance toward unchangeable force turns affliction into instruction?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. What cannot be changed can still be understood and loved.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is necessity accepted. Refusal adds a second suffering on top of the first.
items.lessonContent:
Some forces do not yield.
Understanding replaces struggle.
Acceptance is not approval.
Learn from what resists you.
Share this: accept one immovable fact and ask what it teaches.

items.title: Beyond Personality
items.question: In the factory, Weil found something sacred that belongs to no one; what two-word good names it?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. The sacred appears where personality drops away, in work done well and suffering borne.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is impersonal good. It belongs to no ego, which is why attention can meet it anywhere.
items.lessonContent:
The sacred need not be personal.
Drop the ego to see it.
Work can reveal it.
Look past personalities.
Share this: notice one good thing that belongs to no one.

items.title: Fruitful Emptiness
items.question: Weil says grace needs an empty place to enter; what two-word opening must be kept?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. A kept emptiness lets something other than the self arrive.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is the void. Fullness repels grace, while emptiness receives it.
items.lessonContent:
Emptiness can be fertile.
Do not fill every gap.
Leave room for the unexpected.
Guard one inner silence.
Share this: keep one unscheduled gap in your day.

items.title: Pain Held Well
items.question: When pain cannot be removed, what posture toward affliction keeps attention intact?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. Held rather than fled, suffering can clarify instead of merely crushing.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is affliction embraced. Flight scatters attention, while steady holding preserves it.
items.lessonContent:
Bearing differs from fleeing.
Steadiness preserves sight.
Do not add flight to pain.
Hold still and look.
Share this: stay present through one small discomfort today.

items.title: Need for Roots
items.question: Weil's book on obligations says humans wither without participation and place; what single need names this?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. People need real membership in a living community and a place they belong.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is rootedness. Uprooted lives drift, while planted ones can grow.
items.lessonContent:
Belonging nourishes growth.
Uprooting starves the soul.
Participation matters more than slogans.
Plant yourself somewhere real.
Share this: take part in one local, living community this week.

items.title: Duties First
items.question: Which ordering does Weil insist on: what is owed to others comes before what claims?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. Rights are recognised through the obligations others owe, not claimed first.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is obligations before rights. Starting from duty grounds justice in what is owed.
items.lessonContent:
Duty can ground entitlement.
Start from what is owed.
Claims follow obligations.
Reframe a demand as a debt.
Share this: name one obligation you owe before pressing a right.

items.title: Looking, Not Hunting
items.question: A scientist watches a specimen for an hour without hypothesis; what discipline is she practising?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. She attends to what is there instead of hunting for a desired result.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is attention without seeking. Hypothesis can wait until the object has shown itself.
items.lessonContent:
Hypothesis can blind observation.
Look before theorizing.
Patience reveals detail.
Suspend the search to see.
Share this: observe one thing for five minutes with no goal.

items.title: Saying Yes Truly
items.question: What three-word consent heals the quarrel between desire and the world?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. Saying yes to what is ends the war between wanting and being.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is consent to reality. Refusal keeps the quarrel alive, while consent dissolves it.
items.lessonContent:
Wanting wars with being.
Consent ends the quarrel.
Say yes to what is.
Then act within it.
Share this: consent to one fact you have been refusing.

items.title: World Well Ordered
items.question: Weil finds the universe worthy of love when seen as arranged, not random; what attachment names this?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. Perceived order invites love, while chaos invites only fear or use.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is love of order. Seeing arrangement makes the world lovable rather than merely usable.
items.lessonContent:
Order invites love.
Chaos invites fear.
Look for arrangement first.
Love follows recognition.
Share this: find one ordered pattern in nature today.

items.title: Lovely Trapdoor
items.question: A landscape stops a hurried worker; what role does beauty play in drawing the soul upward?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. Beauty arrests the hurried soul and turns it toward what is higher.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is beauty as lure. It does not merely please; it redirects attention upward.
items.lessonContent:
Beauty interrupts hurry.
Interruption can redirect the soul.
Let loveliness do its work.
Pause when arrested.
Share this: stop for one beautiful thing instead of passing it.

items.title: Fairness Is Seeing
items.question: A supervisor truly sees each worker's difficulty before deciding; what equation does Weil draw?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. To judge justly is first to see clearly, and seeing clearly is attention.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is justice as attention. Rules without regard miss the person they govern.
items.lessonContent:
Judgment needs sight first.
Rules alone cannot see persons.
Attend before deciding.
Let the case appear fully.
Share this: look fully at one person before judging a situation.

items.title: Lesson in Regard
items.question: What method forms students by training the faculty of attention rather than storing results?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. Exercises matter for the attention they train, whatever the answers.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is teaching by attention. Results fade, but the trained faculty remains.
items.lessonContent:
Exercises train more than answers.
Attention outlasts information.
Teach the faculty, not just facts.
Value the effort of looking.
Share this: do one exercise for the attention it trains.

items.title: Hidden Sacred
items.question: Each person carries something untouchable that attention can honour; what three-word reality names it?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. Something in each person calls for reverence rather than use.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is sacred in others. Attention honours it; exploitation violates it.
items.lessonContent:
Persons exceed their uses.
Reverence differs from appraisal.
Honour what cannot be priced.
Look for the untouchable.
Share this: treat one person today as more than their function.

items.title: Holier Part
items.question: Weil distinguishes the personal ego from what holier part of a human being?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. Beyond personality lies the part that can meet truth and justice.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is the impersonal. The ego claims, while this part receives.
items.lessonContent:
Personality is not the whole.
Something holier lies beyond it.
Meet others past their persona.
Seek the impersonal in yourself.
Share this: address one person past their surface traits.

items.title: No Added Stories
items.question: Grief tempts the mind to decorate absence; what discipline stops consolation from falsifying loss?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. Unchecked imagination softens loss into something untrue.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is refusing to imagine. True attention lets absence remain absent rather than filling it.
items.lessonContent:
Imagination can falsify grief.
Consolation may cost truth.
Let absence stay absent.
Look without decorating.
Share this: meet one loss without softening its edges.

items.title: Lowered Eyes
items.question: A reader slows down and lets a difficult page remain difficult; what modest practice is this?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. Humility before the object lets it show itself on its own terms.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is humble observation. Mastery that rushes ahead misses what patience would reveal.
items.lessonContent:
Humility aids perception.
Mastery can rush past truth.
Slow down before difficulty.
Let the object set the pace.
Share this: reread one hard passage slowly without forcing it.

items.title: Slow Respect
items.question: When a friend suffers and no action is possible, what quiet stance remains?
items.correctExplanation: Yes. Waiting with the sufferer honours them when fixing is impossible.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is patient regard. Useless action would serve the helper, while attention serves the friend.
items.lessonContent:
Action is not always the answer.
Presence can be the gift.
Wait rather than fix.
Respect the limits of help.
Share this: keep company with one trouble you cannot solve.
